props.title: One Wonderful Sunday
props.initialSlug: Young couple's bittersweet date in postwar Tokyo

sections.content: **One Wonderful Sunday (1947)** (1947) marks a crucial turning point in Akira Kurosawa's early career, bridging his post-war neorealist phase with his later masterworks. The film follows a young couple struggling in devastated post-war Tokyo, echoing the stark realism of contemporaries like **Germany Year Zero** (1948) and **Bicycle Thieves** (1948). Kurosawa's intimate portrayal of Yuzo and Masako's date on a meager 35 yen budget captures both the crushing poverty and resilient spirit of occupied Japan, while experimenting with fourth-wall breaks that would influence films like **Breathless** (1960).

sections.content: The film's innovative breaking of the fourth wall - particularly in the symphony scene where Masako implores the audience to imagine the music - represents a radical departure from contemporary Japanese cinema. This technique wouldn't become common until the French New Wave, with films like **Jules and Jim** (1962) and **Band of Outsiders** (1964). The couple's struggles to find entertainment on a tight budget mirror similar themes in Italian Neorealism, though Kurosawa infuses more hope and whimsy than contemporaries like **Rome, Open City** (1945).

Beyond its technical innovations, **One Wonderful Sunday** showcases Kurosawa's masterful blend of Western and Japanese influences. The film's baseball sequence and dance hall scenes reflect American cultural infiltration post-occupation, while maintaining distinctly Japanese emotional restraint reminiscent of Ozu's **Record of a Tenement Gentleman** (1947). This cultural hybridization would become a hallmark of Japanese New Wave cinema, influencing directors like Nagisa Oshima and Shohei Imamura. SUBHEAD: Post-War Urban Romance

movies.title: Drunken Angel
movies.slug: Kurosawa's first collaboration with Toshiro Mifune, set in Tokyo's seedy post-war black markets

sections.content: The film's portrayal of young love amid economic hardship created a template for urban romance that resonates through Japanese cinema. Later works like **When a Woman Ascends the Stairs** (1960) and **She and He** (1963) would build on Kurosawa's sensitive depiction of couples navigating financial constraints. The apartment-hunting sequence particularly influenced contemporary Japanese filmmakers like Hirokazu Kore-eda's **Still Walking** (2008) and **After Life** (1998).
